newsitem.title: USA: FBI chief Freeh departs for talks on Saudi bombing.
newsitem.headline: FBI chief Freeh departs for talks on Saudi bombing.

text.p: FBI Director Louis Freeh departed on Friday for Saudi Arabia for meetings with Saudi leaders and additional discussions about the investigation into the June 25 truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. servicemen.
The FBI in a brief statement confirmed the visit, which had been arranged at the invitation of the Saudi government, and described it as "part of an ongoing effort to solve this heinous crime."
"This is a positive meeting, not a scolding," one FBI official said in describing the trip, the third by Freeh to Saudi Arabia since the bombing. "This is a cordial visit, not to pound the table."

FBI officials previously had complained about a lack of cooperation from Saudi authorities in the investigation into the bombing at the U.S. military housing complex in Dhahran. They said FBI agents were not allowed to question Saudi citizens and were not told about any arrests.
The official said Saudi authorities wanted to update Freeh on the progress of their investigation.
In its statement, the FBI said the visit "comes in the context of U.S. support for Saudi efforts to solve this heinous crime."
It added, "FBI agents have been and remain in Saudi Arabia to continue working with Saudi law enforcement authorities on the bombing investigation."

But FBI officials said only a handful of agents remained in Saudi Arabia working on the investigation, down from more than 70 agents who initially had been sent to the Middle Eastern nation to help examine evidence and investigate suspects.
The FBI in its three-paragraph statement emphasised that it was supporting the Saudi investigation.
But Clinton administration officials privately have expressed little hope that any suspects would ever be turned over for prosecution in the United States.

Defence Secretary William Perry told reporters on Nov. 1 the United States has not yet concluded who was responsible for the bombing. He is due to visit Saudi Arabia next weekend as part of a trip to a number of foreign nations around the world.
Diplomatic sources in early November confirmed a Washington Post report that Saudi authorities were holding about 40 Saudi citizens believed to have been implicated in the bombing.

The newspaper reported that Saudi authorities were convinced Iran backed a broad conspiracy in the attack. Iran rejected the charges as "a new U.S. conspiracy to create internal conflict in Islamic-Arabic countries."
